newsitem.title: USA: White House official testifies on Whitewater.
newsitem.headline: White House official testifies on Whitewater.

text.p: White House personnel director Bob Nash, a longtime ally of President Clinton, appeared Tuesday before a Whitewater grand jury investigating Clinton's personal and business finances.
Nash testified for more than three hours before the federal grand jury in Little Rock, but sidestepped reporters' questions at the end of the session.
Nash last year told the Senate Whitewater Committee that he was present at a 1986 meeting between Clinton and James McDougal, the Arkansas businessman at the heart of the Whitewater saga.

Republicans on the Senate committee were sceptical about Nash's claims that no susbtantive matters were discussed at the meeting, which he said was impromptu and involved little more than chit-chat about blue jeans.
The meeting took place in McDougal's office at an Arkansas real estate project known as Castle Grande.

Investigators are trying to determine whether first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton, who has acknowledged performing some legal work for McDougal's savings and loan on the project, helped him buy the Castle Grande property in what regulators say was a "sham transaction".
Hillary Clinton has flatly denied any wrongdoing.
McDougal and the Clintons were partners in the ill-fated Whitewater real estate venture in northern Arkansas.
The transaction is part of several legal proceedings arising from the failure of the Madison Savings and Loan Association, which cost taxpayers an estimated $65 million.

The Clintons entered into a partnership with the McDougals in the Whitewater real estate venture in 1978. Although their investment lost money, questions have arisen about whether funds for the project were siphoned from the savings and loan, which was also a McDougal holding.
Nash was an economic development aide in Arkansas when Clinton was state governor and the two men are close friends.
McDougal's attorney, Sam Heuer, was also called in to testify before the grand jury Tuesday.

McDougal was convicted in May last year on 18 counts of fraud and conspiracy, but then began cooperating with independent prosecutor Kenneth Starr and has reportedly corroborated allegations of improper behaviour by the Clintons.
In return for his cooperation, McDougal was last month sentenced to three years in prison and three years probation. He had faced a possible maximum sentence of 81 years.
A federal judge Monday turned down his request to remain free while his convictions were appealed, and he must report to prison June 16.
